title: The prophets, looking back
hookLine: justice like a river, and a God who won't forget
tomorrow: who hears 'great joy' first in Luke? not who you'd guess.

lines: WHY TELL A CHOIR TO STOP?
cards: The worship night was incredible: lights low, phones in the air, the bridge sung three times through. Now an odd verse.
In the book of Amos, God says to people at worship: “Take thou away from me the noise of thy songs; for I will not hear the melody of thy viols.” Noise. Their best music, called noise.
Why would God ever tell a choir to stop singing?

teach.b: Read around the verse, and the puzzle solves itself. Amos was a herdsman from Tekoa who said he was no prophet, and no prophet's son.
He spoke to people whose songs were rising while, in his words, their treading was upon the poor. The singing wasn't the problem.
The singing was covering for something.
So the very next line says what God wants instead: “But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.” Not a trickle on a feast day. A river that keeps coming.
Micah folds it into one sentence: “what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?” Looking back, the prophets aren't fortune tellers.

They're truth tellers to their own day, about the widow, the orphan, the poor and the stranger. And they don't only warn. Isaiah says a mother may forget her nursing child, “yet will I not forget thee.”

teach.h: HAVE WE NOT ALL ONE FATHER?
teach.b: Malachi asks the question underneath it all: “Have we not all one father? hath not one God created us?”
If one God made everyone, the stranger at the gate is family. Something to repeat at dinner: Martin Luther King Jr. reached for Amos's river line in his speeches.
Jews and Christians both read these books as scripture, and Christians also hear them pointing toward Jesus.

how: Christians read the prophets in worship, especially in Advent, and some churches turn their words into work for the poor and the stranger; Jews read the prophets in the synagogue alongside the Torah.

o: truth tellers who called people to justice and mercy
fortune tellers who mainly predicted the far future

games.q: who said what — tap the pairs.
p: let judgment run down as waters
do justly, love mercy, walk humbly
yet will I not forget thee

s: the Bible's prophets were mainly fortune tellers
they were truth tellers to their own day, about the poor, the widow and the stranger.
in Amos, God calls the worshippers' songs noise
"take thou away from me the noise of thy songs", while the poor were trampled.
the next line asks for justice like a river. the songs were covering for something.

games.q: your youth group is raising money for a new sound system. down the street, the food pantry is short on volunteers this month. what would Amos ask first?
o: drop the sound system; God doesn't want music.
keep the songs, and keep the river of justice moving too.
the music is worship, so it comes before everything else.
games.why: Amos's problem wasn't the music; it was music covering for trampling the poor. let judgment run down as waters, and the songs ring true.

practice: A small plan for doing justice. Name one thing near you that isn't fair and is yours to touch: a chore always left to the same person, a friend who keeps getting talked over, money you owe.
Then name what usually stops you, and one plain step past it, small enough for this week. If you pray, hold that step up with Micah's words: do justly, love mercy, walk humbly.

wordCard.voice: The prophets. Amos, Micah, Isaiah, Malachi and others: truth tellers who asked for justice like a river, and spoke of a God who won't forget.

orig.note: Hebrew: justice, setting things right. the word behind 'judgment' in Amos 5:24.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: justice and mercy, side by side in one sentence of Micah's. A river, not a trickle.
